title: What Is Appraisal?
description: The contractual process that resolves disputes over the amount of a covered loss.
whenToUse: Reference this any time you or a client need a plain-language explanation of appraisal.
content:
Appraisal is a contractual dispute-resolution process built into most property insurance policies. It resolves disagreements over the amount of a covered loss — not whether the loss is covered in the first place. Both sides have to already agree the damage is covered; appraisal exists purely to settle the dollar value of the repair or replacement.

Each party selects its own independent appraiser. The two appraisers then select a neutral third party called an umpire. The appraisers try to agree on the amount of loss between themselves; if they can't, the disagreement is submitted to the umpire. An agreement between any two of the three (the two appraisers, or one appraiser and the umpire) becomes the binding amount of loss.

Appraisal is generally faster and less expensive than a lawsuit, and the resulting award is typically binding on both sides. Each party usually pays its own appraiser, with the umpire's fee often split evenly — though the exact terms come from the specific policy's appraisal clause, which can vary by carrier and state.

title: What Is ITEL (and RLS / NTS)?
description: Third-party services that determine whether a roofing material is available or discontinued.
whenToUse: Reference this when a claim involves a material-matching or availability dispute.
content:
ITEL (and similar services like RLS or NTS) are third-party reporting services used in the roofing industry to determine whether a specific shingle or material is still available, discontinued, or a reasonable match to existing product. A report from one of these services is often used to support an argument for full-slope or full-roof replacement when a repair alone would leave a visible, undocumented mismatch.

These reports carry weight with carriers because they come from an independent third party rather than the contractor's own opinion — which is exactly why they're useful in a documentation-based reconsideration request.

title: What Is a NOA / Hail Impact Report?
description: Documentation that ties storm damage to a specific date and location.
whenToUse: Reference this when a carrier disputes whether storm damage actually occurred, or when countering a wear-and-tear or prior-damage argument.
content: A NOA (Notice of Award, in some contexts) or hail impact report generally refers to storm/weather documentation — data showing that a hail, wind, or other storm event occurred at a specific property on a specific date, and with what intensity. This kind of report is useful for tying damage directly to a dated event, which helps counter arguments that damage is wear and tear, age-related, or pre-existing.

title: What Is Reinspection?
description: A follow-up inspection requested when damage may have been missed or undervalued.
whenToUse: Reference this to explain the reinspection process to a newer specialist or a client.
content: Reinspection is a request for the carrier to send an adjuster back to the property to review damage that wasn't captured, or wasn't fully captured, in the original inspection. It's typically appropriate when there's a specific, documented basis to believe something was missed — not as a general "look again" request. A well-supported reinspection request names the exact items in dispute and includes documentation (photos, measurements) up front.

title: Wear and Tear vs. Storm Damage
description: How carriers distinguish gradual deterioration from a covered storm event.
whenToUse: Reference this when preparing a response to a wear-and-tear or age-related denial.
content:
Most property policies exclude damage caused by gradual wear and tear or normal aging, while covering sudden, accidental damage from a specific storm event. Carriers will sometimes attribute roof damage to wear and tear (or age) rather than a specific storm, which limits or eliminates coverage.

The strongest counter to this argument usually combines two things: documentation tying the damage to a specific storm event (date, location, intensity), and photo evidence showing damage patterns consistent with impact (bruising, fractures, granule loss in a pattern) rather than gradual deterioration.

title: What Is "Matching"?
description: The question of whether replacement material needs to reasonably match existing, undamaged material.
whenToUse: Reference this when a claim involves a dispute over whether a partial repair would leave a visible mismatch.
content: "Matching" refers to the question of whether repair materials need to reasonably match adjacent, undamaged materials in color, texture, or appearance. This becomes a coverage and scope question when the original material is discontinued or otherwise unavailable — repairing only the damaged section could leave a visible, mismatched result. Some states have specific matching statutes or regulatory guidance that carriers must follow; specifics vary by state and by carrier, so confirm current requirements with your lead when a matching argument is central to a claim.

title: Actual Cash Value (ACV) vs. Replacement Cost Value (RCV)
description: The two ways a covered loss can be valued, and why payment amounts sometimes look lower than expected.
whenToUse: Reference this when a client questions why a payment amount seems low.
content:
Replacement Cost Value (RCV) is the cost to repair or replace damaged property with new materials of similar kind and quality, without a deduction for depreciation. Actual Cash Value (ACV) is RCV minus depreciation — an adjustment for the age and condition of the damaged property.

Many policies pay ACV first, and release the depreciation (the difference between ACV and RCV, called "recoverable depreciation") once the repair is completed and documented. This is a common and often legitimate reason a first payment looks lower than the full estimate.

title: What Is a Supplement?
description: A request to add items or adjust pricing on an already-approved estimate.
whenToUse: Reference this when specific items are missing from an otherwise-approved estimate.
content: A supplement is a request to add missing items, correct quantities, or adjust pricing on a claim that's already been approved — as opposed to challenging the entire scope or reopening a denial. Supplements are typically used for more targeted, factual corrections (a missed line item, an incorrect measurement) rather than broad disagreements, which are more often resolved through pushing the estimate or appraisal.

title: Recoverable vs. Non-Recoverable Depreciation
description: Whether withheld depreciation can be recovered after the repair is completed.
whenToUse: Reference this alongside ACV vs. RCV when explaining a payment breakdown to a client.
content: Recoverable depreciation is the portion of value withheld from an initial ACV payment that can be claimed back once the repair is completed and documented (often by submitting a final invoice). Non-recoverable depreciation is withheld permanently and never paid out, regardless of whether the repair is completed — this depends on the specific policy language. Always check the policy itself rather than assuming; this varies by carrier and by policy.

title: What Is an Appraisal Umpire?
description: The neutral third party who resolves a disagreement between the two appraisers.
whenToUse: Reference this when explaining the appraisal process, especially if the two appraisers reach an impasse.
content: An umpire is a neutral third party selected by the two parties' appraisers (or, if they can't agree, sometimes by a court) once appraisal has been invoked. The umpire's role is specifically to resolve disagreements between the two appraisers on the amount of loss. If the appraisers can't agree on a number, the dispute goes to the umpire, and an agreement between any two of the three (the two appraisers, or one appraiser and the umpire) becomes the binding award. Reaching the umpire stage is a normal part of the process, not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

title: State Farm's 10-Day Pre-Appraisal Notice Rule
description: What State Farm's 10-day appraisal condition actually requires, why demands get rejected under it, and how to make sure it never costs us time.
whenToUse: Read this before sending any appraisal demand on a State Farm claim, and any time State Farm rejects a demand as 'premature' or 'not itemized.'
content:
WHAT THE POLICY SAYS
State Farm's newer homeowners forms (the HW-21xx series, e.g., HW-2122 Michigan and HW-2136 Oklahoma) and the FE-5626 Amendatory Appraisal Endorsement replaced the old one-paragraph appraisal clause. The new condition includes a requirement that, at least 10 days before demanding appraisal, the party seeking appraisal give the other party written, itemized documentation of a specific dispute as to the amount of the loss, identifying separately each item being disputed. It also requires the insured to have complied with the policy's duties after loss, and it gives each side 20 days after receiving a written demand to name its appraiser. The exact wording varies by state and form, so always read the endorsement on the actual policy.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY
The condition doesn't mention reinspection. The 10 days run from State Farm's receipt of the itemized dispute, not from a reinspection request and not from State Farm's reinspection decision. Denying the reinspection the next day neither stops nor restarts the clock. If our reinspection request was itemized and State Farm provably received it, day 10 is the same no matter what State Farm does with the reinspection. In practice, the 'wait 10 days after the reinspection request' rule is only true because the reinspection request is usually the first itemized dispute we send.

HOW STATE FARM WINS THESE (AND HOW WE STOP IT)
1. Demand sent too early. Fix: never send a State Farm demand before day 12 after confirmed receipt of the itemized notice. (That's a 2-day buffer over the minimum, so day-counting arguments don't matter.)
2. No proof of receipt. In a March 2026 Eastern District of Pennsylvania decision, State Farm won summary judgment on the appraisal claim and the bad-faith claim. The insured couldn't show State Farm received the estimate before the demand went out. Fix: get a portal upload confirmation, the adjuster's reply, or certified-mail tracking for every itemized notice, and attach it to the demand.
3. 'Not itemized.' A contractor estimate attached with no comparison invites this argument. Fix: list each disputed line separately with State Farm's amount, our amount, and the reason. Use the Reinspection Request + Itemized Dispute Notice template.
4. 'Scope/causation is a coverage issue, not amount of loss.' State Farm has used this to refuse appraisal (e.g., Hart v. State Farm in Michigan, Zhao v. State Farm in Illinois). This is separate from the 10-day rule. Escalate it rather than handling it as a timing problem.

THE WORKFLOW THAT TAKES THE 10 DAYS OFF THE TABLE
- Day 0: Send the reinspection request as the Reinspection Request + Itemized Dispute Notice. Get proof of receipt and log the receipt date in Contractors Cloud.
- Day 1-11: Whatever State Farm does with the reinspection (deny, ignore, schedule), prepare the appraisal package in parallel: appraiser selected, client authorization signed.
- Day 12+: If the dispute isn't resolved, send the 10-Day-Compliant Appraisal Demand, stating the notice receipt date and attaching proof.
- If State Farm rejects a demand as premature: if 10+ days have passed since receipt (they almost always have by then), re-serve the same day. Respond in writing only if the original demand was actually compliant.

STATE-LAW EXCEPTIONS
In Hart v. State Farm (E.D. Mich. 2021), the court held that most of the appraisal provisions in Michigan form HW-2122 were void because they were more burdensome than Michigan's statutory standard fire policy appraisal language (MCL 500.2833). Other states with a statutory standard fire policy may support similar arguments. These are legal questions, so escalate Michigan files and any file where we want to challenge the clause itself. Don't just ignore the clause. Outside those situations, assume courts will enforce the 10-day condition as written. The winning move is to comply early and keep proof of receipt, not to fight the rule.

This article is internal process guidance, not legal advice. Policy wording varies by state and form, so confirm the endorsement on the actual policy.
